beats.title: The claim
beats.heading: The claim
beats.sub: Encrypted · versioned · scoped to one run · a written mandate: each number read from data/vaults.json and data/report.json
beats.say: rUv's stack gives agents swarms, consensus, self-learning and speed, with its own policy engine and memory. What we add is a memory with history, and a mandate. Here a worker learns something. It is encrypted before it leaves the agent, so the server only ever holds ciphertext: zero plaintext found, across every run. It is versioned, so you know who learned what, and when. It is scoped to one run: the vault is measured, then deleted. And a mandate, written down, compiled into Ruflo's own policy engine: six of eleven actions stopped. Tonight is mostly about the memory.

beats.title: Memory: what RuVector secures, and where sgit adds
beats.heading: RuVector secures the memory; sgit wraps the files
beats.sub: RuVector README, "Security and governance" (github.com/ruvnet/ruvector, main branch, read 15 Oct 2026) · sgit figures from data/vaults.json
beats.say: Start with the memory. RuVector is a remarkable memory substrate: vectors, graphs, full snapshots, even copy-on-write branches. And its README has a clear section on security and governance. Its witness logs are tamper evident, and it says, just as plainly, that they do not encrypt memory content, and that a delete does not automatically reach every snapshot, branch or copy, so define retention and erasure across every copy. That is where sgit adds, around the files: encrypted on the client, AES-256-GCM, so the server only ever stores ciphertext; a history you can clone anywhere; and a vault that is deleted with the run, and checked: no store paths left, and a clone with the key fails.

beats.title: What an sgit vault is
beats.heading: What an sgit vault is
beats.sub: git for encrypted vaults: encrypted on the client, versioned like git, ephemeral when you want · sgit-ai 0.21.0 · timings from data/vaults.json
beats.say: So what is an sgit vault? It's git for encrypted vaults. A folder on your machine; every file is encrypted on the client, AES-256-GCM, before anything leaves, so the server only ever stores ciphertext. Whoever has the vault key has the memory. And it works like git: commit, branch, merge, push, clone, each about a second against our local vault server. For agents, that's a shared, versioned memory across machines: a fresh clone anywhere gets the whole history back. Or make it ephemeral: one vault per run, deleted at the end, and we check the delete.

beats.title: What an Agent Behaviour Policy is
beats.heading: What an Agent Behaviour Policy is
beats.sub: A written mandate per role, compiled into Ruflo's own policy engine, with receipts
beats.say: This is an Agent Behaviour Policy: a written mandate, per role, that a person can read. One row per capability, in a small grammar of 23 primitives: verb, object, reach. Each row says yes, no or ask a human, why, and the barrier. It has an owner and an end date. We don't build a new enforcer: it compiles into Ruflo's own policy engine, rUv's, in enforce mode: 36 rules. Then real actions hit it. In POC1, 6 of 11 were stopped: 4 denied, 2 sent to a human. Every decision went into a hash-chained receipt, and the chain is valid.

beats.title: ruv.sgit: one hive, one vault, one run
beats.sub: ruv.sgit: a Ruflo hive + sgit vaults + Agent Behaviour Policies
beats.caption: The layers · made by ruv.sgit run r3-define · policy outcomes from POC1, vault from run r2-materials
beats.say: So put the two together. ruv.sgit is a Ruflo hive plus sgit vaults plus Agent Behaviour Policies: a queen and workers in parallel, one ephemeral vault per run, and a written mandate for what each worker may do. Each worker's delivery lands on its own branch; the branches merge; the run is measured into a ledger; and then the vault is deleted. Memory that exists for exactly as long as the work does, with a receipt afterwards. Tonight's three new pages, and this script, were made by one such run: run r2-materials, five workers, on a local vault server.

beats.title: Vault lanes
beats.caption: Studio v3 · vault lanes: one lane per agent role, commits, merges, a fresh clone · an illustration built in studio run 1
beats.say: Here's the shape of it, as an illustration. One lane per agent role: that lane is a branch of the vault. Each dot is a commit, encrypted before it is uploaded. The lanes merge into the main line, which sgit calls current. And at the end, a fresh clone, into an empty folder, pulls the whole history back. The server held ciphertext throughout. Whoever has the key has the memory, and nobody else does, including the host.

beats.title: Memory with history
beats.heading: One run's vault, commit by commit
beats.sub: ruv.sgit run r5-market, 15 Oct 2026 · POC2, 14 Oct 2026 · sgit times as measured
beats.say: This is a real run's vault, from this afternoon. The brief lands on current. Then each worker gets its own branch, commits what it delivered, and merges back: who, what, when, and how long each sgit step took, in milliseconds. Now the flow: six workers, eight commits, encrypted on the client before the push. The server holds ciphertext only: we searched it for forty fragments of the text and found none. A fresh clone came back identical, and then the vault was deleted, with nothing left. Memory works the same way. In POC2, run locally, a coder and a tester each wrote their Ruflo memory to the vault; the folder was deleted, a fresh clone restored it, and Ruflo gave the same answers. Every step is a commit, and it's gone when the run is.

beats.title: ruv.sgit in motion
beats.caption: ruv.sgit in motion · a real run, drawn from its entry in data/vaults.json
beats.say: This is ruv.sgit in motion, drawn from a real run's entry in the ledger, not a mock-up. The run opens: the hive starts, the vault is created, and the brief is committed. The workers start in parallel. Each delivery lands on its own branch, is pushed, and merges into current. Every sgit call and every Ruflo call is timed and recorded as it happens. Then the close: the vault is measured, cloned fresh, and checked against what the workers delivered. Then it's gone. Watch the branches: the workers work in parallel, nobody writes on anyone else's branch, and the deliveries merge one at a time. The merge is where the work meets, and the history keeps who did what.

beats.title: How to read the ledger
beats.heading: The vault ledger: one row per run
beats.sub: Every number read at load from data/vaults.json, written after each run by poc/ruv-sgit/ruvsgit.py
beats.say: Every run leaves one row in a ledger. Here's how to read one. The run, and what it was for. The workers, each writing on its own branch. The commits. What they delivered, and what the server held: all ciphertext. Then the probe: fragments of the delivered files, searched for in every byte the server stored. Plaintext found: zero. A fresh clone with the key: identical. Then the vault is deleted, and we check: nothing left in the store, and a clone fails. Now every run, and the totals. Ephemeral: every vault deleted after its numbers were recorded.
beats.cue: Point at the plaintext-found cell, then the ephemeral line.

Three of them are in this talk; all seven are on the site. Which brings us to the wall.

beats.title: Same 11 actions, default against the ABP
beats.caption: POC1 · the same trace evaluated twice, recorded 14 Oct 2026 · data/report.json
beats.say: So we write it down: an Agent Behaviour Policy, one row per capability, compiled into Ruflo's own engine. The same eleven actions, played twice. On the left, the default: all allowed. On the right, the mandate: email denied, pastebin denied, the tester editing source denied, the researcher reading AWS credentials denied; and the push and the deploy wait for a human. Six of eleven stopped, five allowed, every reason names its row, and every decision is a hash-chained receipt.

beats.title: Four ways to work with us
beats.heading: Four offers. Mix and match.
beats.sub: Task runs, dedicated compute, a maintained repository, expert time: all built on a Ruflo hive + sgit vaults + Agent Behaviour Policies
beats.say: If you want to use this, there are four ways. One: a task run on our infrastructure. You send a brief and your materials. A Ruflo queen and her workers do the work inside an ephemeral sgit vault, each role under its own behaviour policy, with no internet, and you get the vault back as a zip or published. Ten, twenty or fifty pounds a run, a bit less with your own model key. Two: dedicated compute, a machine started for your task with the vault created inside it. Three: a private repository of the whole setup, kept up to date by us, from 149 pounds a month up to white label. Four: time with us, from a couple of hours to several days. They mix and match. Consultants can white label it, companies can add it to what they sell, and internal teams can run it inside. Anybody who implements this implements sgit vaults and Agent Behaviour Policies.
